title: Crimson Desert and the Joys of Digital Tourism
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fnKAo4k4j0I

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a confession: he wrote a scathing review of Crimson Desert for Patreon at launch, bounced off it hard — and then bought it a second time. The base PS5 version ran and looked poorly enough that he won't recommend it there at all; a low-end PC at 1080p with Ray Reconstruction on finally gave him a stable 60fps and a world he wanted to live in.

What hooked him is this channel's usual preoccupation, transplanted. He calls it digital tourism, and compares the world directly to a big open-world hex crawl on the tabletop — he has hundreds of hours in Skyrim and never finished it, and doesn't intend to finish this either. The click moment came off-quest: a puzzle opened a giant fan, he deployed his wings, rode the air current up to one of the floating sky islands and fought a boss nothing had sent him to find. Combat sits closer to Dynasty Warriors than Souls, and gear modifiers swap freely between weapons, so you can equip whatever looks best.

He is not selling it as a masterpiece. The first ten hours are chores, the controls are cumbersome and over-layered, and puzzles won't tell you when you simply lack the ability yet. Every puzzle pays the same skill point; every waterfall cave holds the same kind of chest. Quests don't snowball the way Skyrim's did.

----

Daniel's favourite find was a hidden room with no map marker, no quest, and no purpose he could identify — and he loved it precisely for that. Does exploration need to be rewarded, or is being worth looking at enough?
